strengths: The paper contributes a useful, NLP-relevant resource: 20,281 preference pairs constructed from naturally occurring conversational feedback, with additional versions generated by three policy models. Connecting user dissatisfaction to preference-data construction is a practical contribution.

Experiments across Phi-3, LLaMA-3, and Qwen2 demonstrate substantial improvements over the starting instruction-tuned models on established benchmarks. For example, Phi-3’s AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate improves from 24.3% to 34.9%, and its Arena-Hard win rate improves from 15.4% to 32.4%. These results support the dataset’s training utility.

The evaluation includes regenerated UltraFeedback baselines, a 540-example test set reportedly separated by conversation and user, and human validation of both feedback classification and checklist judging. These are meaningful methodological safeguards.

The dataset link, detailed prompts, model identifiers, and core SFT/DPO hyperparameters provide a reasonable basis for reproduction. The supported resource and training results warrant Findings consideration.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the benefit of using actual user feedback. WildFeedback and UltraFeedback differ in prompt distribution, conversation length, rejected-response construction, and filtering. A baseline using the same WildChat prompts and generation procedure without feedback conditioning is missing. Consequently, the gains cannot confidently be attributed to feedback-derived preferences rather than other dataset differences.

The stronger claim of improved alignment with actual users remains insufficiently validated. GPT-4-family models extract preferences, generate or filter responses, and judge outputs, creating potential correlated biases. Appendix C reports 57.14% judge–human agreement and κ=0.372 on 200 conversations, which provides some validation but does not establish that checklists improve agreement over judging without checklists. There is also no direct human comparison of the final trained models or measurement of user satisfaction.

Claims of significant and consistent superiority over UltraFeedback overstate Table 3. For Qwen2 with GPT-4-generated data, WildFeedback performs worse on AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate (39.4 versus 40.6) and MT-Bench (7.60 versus 7.66). Several other advantages are small, and confidence intervals or repeated training runs are absent. Improvements over the starting models are more convincing than universal superiority over the competing dataset.

The evaluation supports a narrower population claim than the paper makes. Selecting central preferences within clusters deliberately excludes less common preferences and does not establish representation of the majority of users. Dissatisfaction-focused sampling and DSAT recall of 48.4% further restrict coverage. The acknowledged selection bias should qualify claims about diverse human values and overcoming subjectivity or synthetic-data bias.

Some consequential reproduction details remain unspecified, including generation settings, the embedding and selection configuration for the clustered test set, and whether preference-derived system instructions are retained in training inputs. The hyperparameter search also lacks a stated validation and selection protocol. Clarifying these details would strengthen confidence in the comparisons.
